The cell’s pattern recognition receptors scan the cytoplasm for molecular signatures that betray an invader, chief among them double-stranded RNA, and one of the most important sentinels in this surveillance system is the retinoic acid-inducible gene I, known widely as RIG-I. Once RIG-I binds viral RNA, it initiates a signaling cascade that culminates in the production of type I and type III interferons, the cytokines that place neighboring cells on heightened alert and coordinate the antiviral response. SARS-CoV-2, the agent responsible for COVID-19, has proven remarkably adept at delaying or blunting this alarm, and a study published in Virology Journal now adds a detailed mechanism to the growing catalog of its evasion strategies. The work, led by researchers at Guizhou Medical University, focuses on nonstructural protein 14, or NSP14, and reveals how this multifunctional viral enzyme quietly severs a critical partnership that amplifies interferon signaling. NSP14 is one of sixteen nonstructural proteins encoded by the SARS-CoV-2 genome, and it wears two enzymatic hats that are both essential for viral replication. Its N-terminal domain functions as an exoribonuclease, proofreading freshly synthesized viral RNA and excising mismatched nucleotides, while its C-terminal domain acts as an N7-methyltransferase, adding a methyl group to the 5′ cap of viral messenger RNA so that the RNA masquerades as a cellular transcript. This cap modification allows viral RNA to evade detection by innate immune receptors and to be translated efficiently by the host machinery. Previous research had implicated NSP14 in antagonizing interferon responses, but the precise route it takes through the signaling network remained incompletely mapped, particularly with respect to the RIG-I pathway that dominates the sensing of RNA viruses. To dissect this question, the research team employed overexpression systems and reporter assays to test what happens to interferon production when NSP14 is present. The results were unambiguous. Elevated levels of NSP14 significantly suppressed both type I and type III interferon responses, along with the expression of downstream interferon-stimulated genes, the effector proteins that execute much of the antiviral program. The suppression extended to key signaling intermediates: activation of TBK1, the kinase that phosphorylates downstream transcription factors, and activation of IRF3, the transcription factor that drives interferon-beta transcription, were both dampened. In effect, NSP14 was acting upstream of the phosphorylation events that normally convert RNA sensing into gene expression, placing its point of interference early in the RIG-I signaling axis. Discover more Covid-19 Infectious Diseases Medical Literature & Resources Drugs & Medications Respiratory Conditions A central question in such experiments is which part of a viral protein carries out a given function, and the team addressed this by testing whether NSP14’s immunosuppressive effect depended on its catalytic activities or on its interactions with other viral components. NSP14 is known to form a complex with NSP10, a cofactor that stimulates its exoribonuclease activity, and the researchers examined whether this partnership was required. It was not. The inhibitory effect on RIG-I-mediated antiviral signaling persisted independently of complex formation with NSP10. What did matter was the C-terminal N7-methyltransferase activity. When that function was disabled, the ability of NSP14 to suppress interferon production was lost, indicating that the methyltransferase domain is the business end of the immune evasion strategy, even though the mechanism does not appear to operate through cap modification of viral RNA itself. With the functional requirement mapped to the methyltransferase domain, the investigators turned to the question of which host protein NSP14 might be targeting. Using immunoprecipitation followed by mass spectrometry, they searched for cellular interaction partners of NSP14 and identified DHX15, a DEAH-box helicase that had previously been characterized as a co-receptor of RIG-I. DHX15 belongs to the large family of DExD/C-box helicases, enzymes that remodel RNA structures and, in several cases, contribute to innate immune signaling. The finding that a viral enzyme with methyltransferase activity physically contacts DHX15 suggested a plausible bridge between the protein’s known biochemistry and its observed immunological effect. The significance of DHX15 as a target becomes clear when its normal role is considered. Earlier studies had established that DHX15 cooperates with RIG-I to enhance signaling triggered by RNA viruses, functioning as a co-receptor that strengthens the antiviral response. In other words, DHX15 is not merely an accessory protein; it is part of the amplification system that allows the RIG-I pathway to generate a robust interferon signal. A virus that could disrupt the DHX15-RIG-I partnership would effectively turn down the volume of the alarm before it ever reaches the nucleus. The research team set out to test whether NSP14 does exactly that, and their experiments confirmed the hypothesis. Using co-immunoprecipitation assays, the researchers demonstrated that NSP14 dampens the interaction between DHX15 and RIG-I. By binding to DHX15, the viral protein occupies a partner that would otherwise assist RIG-I in propagating the activation signal downstream to MAVS, the mitochondrial antiviral-signaling protein that serves as the platform assembling TBK1 and other signaling components. The consequences of this interference follow a coherent logic: with fewer productive DHX15-RIG-I complexes, reduced activation of TBK1 and IRF3 follows, and the transcription of interferon genes falters. The pathway from viral methyltransferase to blunted cytokine output is thus traced step by step, from protein-protein contact at the level of the sensors to diminished phosphorylation at the level of the kinases to reduced gene expression at the level of the interferon loci. Discover more Biological Sciences CoV-2 Genetics Biotechnology news updates Health Conditions These findings carry several implications for how scientists understand the immune battlefield inside SARS-CoV-2-infected cells. First, they illustrate the economy of viral genomes, in which a single protein performs multiple jobs: the same NSP14 molecule that proofreads and caps the viral RNA also moonlights as an immune antagonist, using its methyltransferase domain for a second, noncanonical purpose. Second, they highlight DHX15 as a newly appreciated node of viral attack, expanding the list of host factors that coronaviruses manipulate and suggesting that the partnership between helicase co-receptors and RIG-I-like receptors is a vulnerability that pathogens have evolved to exploit. Third, they reinforce the picture of SARS-CoV-2 as a virus with a formidable arsenal of evasion strategies, in which early innate immune suppression buys time for viral replication before adaptive immunity can mount an effective response. The study also opens avenues for therapeutic thinking. If NSP14’s N7-methyltransferase activity is required for suppressing interferon production, then inhibitors of that enzymatic function might do double duty, impairing viral RNA capping while simultaneously relieving the brake on innate immunity. Small molecules targeting the methyltransferase domain are already of interest in antiviral drug development, and this work adds an immunological rationale to the enzymatic one. Similarly, approaches that stabilize or mimic the DHX15-RIG-I interaction could, in principle, restore signaling amplitude in infected tissues, although such strategies remain far from clinical application. As with all mechanistic cell culture studies, important caveats apply: the experiments relied on overexpression systems, and confirming that the same interference operates during authentic SARS-CoV-2 infection at physiological protein levels will be an important next step. What the research ultimately delivers is a clearer molecular narrative of how SARS-CoV-2 mutes the body’s first response to infection. The virus does not merely hide its RNA; it actively dismantles the cooperative architecture of the sensing machinery, using NSP14 to pry apart DHX15 and RIG-I and thereby weakening the signal before it can cascade into interferon production. Every element of that cascade, from the helicase partnership at the membrane-associated sensor level to the phosphorylation of TBK1 and IRF3 to the expression of interferon-stimulated genes, is diminished as a result. In mapping this route with biochemical precision, the team at Guizhou Medical University has not only illuminated a specific evasion tactic of a globally significant pathogen but has also underscored a broader lesson of the COVID-19 era: the proteins viruses bring with them are often multitaskers, and understanding their secondary functions may reveal the most consequential battlegrounds of all. content_title: Leon County COVID-19 cases climb as flu season approaches
content: As the new school year begins, Tallahassee students face a looming surge of the flu, COVID-19, and respiratory syncytial virus (RSV). The combination, known as "triple-demic," typically peaks during the cooler winter months. According to the Pandemic Mitigation Collaborative's Sept. 25 update, Leon County's COVID-19 prevalence is high . Cases began climbing after Aug. 15, aligning with the start of the new academic semester at Florida State University, Florida A&M University, and Tallahassee State College. "There is a misconception that COVID 'ended,'" FSU College of Medicine Professor Dr. George Rust said to the FSView. "We've had COVID cases and even deaths continuously since the start of the pandemic. It tends to come in waves, and because of immunizations and some people developing immunity from prior infection, the baseline rates and the seasonal surges are lower than they were in 2021 to 2024, but they persist." Flu cases in Tallahassee currently fall in the low-to-medium range. Historically, Florida's flu season runs from October through May. Rust said the cooler months pose a great risk for "triple-demic" illnesses, including the flu, for several reasons. "Cold, dry air or even indoor heated air (also dry) can help the virus to hang in the air longer and to remain alive on surfaces longer," Rust said. "In addition, drying out the lining of the nose can decrease mucous production that traps germs, and can also diminish the response of immune cells in the nose and respiratory tract." More: What students need to know about the 2026 flu season Rust also noted that colder weather keeps people indoors, increasing face-to-face contact. Holiday travel and gatherings bring people together from different areas, allowing viruses to spread easily in crowded, indoor environments. To curb viral transmissions, local healthcare professionals encourage students to establish simple daily routines. "Washing your hands, covering your cough, and using hand sanitizer after touching the gas pump are some simple and easy habits that work to prevent illness not only during flu season but year-round," Megan Waltman, an infection preventionist and nurse at Tallahassee Memorial HealthCare, said to the FSView. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, washing hands with soap for 20 to 30 seconds effectively stops the spread of germs. The habit can reduce respiratory illnesses, such as colds, in the general population by 16% to 21%. Students can take simple steps to stay safe. FSU Assistant Director of Public Relations & Appointment Scheduling at University Health Services (UHS) Mari Kay Avant told the FSView that several daily habits can prevent the spread of respiratory illness. "Students should wash their hands regularly, get enough sleep, eat balanced meals, stay hydrated, and remain physically active," Avant said to the FSView. "It's also important to avoid sharing drinks, utensils, and other personal items. If you do get sick, stay home and limit close contact with others to help prevent spreading illness to friends, roommates, and others on campus." Flu vaccines are currently offered at UHS at no cost to FSU students. To maximize convenience, UHS will host vaccination clinics across campus this semester. Upcoming outreach includes mobile "Flu-ber" stations and the Be Well, Do Well Health Fair on Landis Green on Oct. 1. More: Florida moves to drop four school vaccine requirements Avant said that students who experience symptoms or have health concerns can visit UHS for treatment. Established, returning patients with Patient Portal access can schedule appointments online . First-time patients must call UHS at 850-644-4567 or visit the clinic in person to book a time. All students must bring their FSUCard and health insurance card to check in. Avant added that students seeking same-day appointments should call early in the morning when opening slots are most available. McKinsey Lamm is a Staff Writer for the FSView & Florida Flambeau, the student-run, independent online news service for the FSU and Tallahassee communities. Email our staff at contact@fsview.com . COVID-19 infections are growing or likely growing in 27 states as of September 16, 2026, according to estimates from the CDC.1 As flu season begins, Tammy Lundstrom, MD, JD, senior vice president and chief medical officer at Trinity Health, said in an interview with The American Journal of Managed Care® that COVID-19 and flu symptoms overlap enough to make the 2 illnesses difficult to tell apart. Fatigue, muscle aches, fever, sore throat, cough, and shortness of breath are all symptoms associated with both COVID-19 and the flu, Lundstrom said. Children in particular may also experience gastrointestinal upset, including nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea, with COVID-19, she added. "Really, it's hard to distinguish just by symptoms what you're dealing with. It really requires a visit," Lundstrom said. To limit spread, she recommended staying home when sick, washing hands frequently, using antimicrobial hand gels, avoiding touching the nose, mouth, and eyes, and covering the mouth and nose when sneezing or coughing. Lundstrom also emphasized vaccination. She recommended the flu vaccine for anyone aged 6 months and older, with a high-dose or recombinant flu vaccine for adults older than 65 years. For COVID-19, she pointed to recommendations from the Infectious Diseases Society of America, the American Medical Association, and the American Academy of Pediatrics. "Anybody over the age of 19 should get vaccinated. Those 6 months of age to 23 months should be vaccinated for COVID," she explained. "And then older children are really based on their risk profile. And definitely, supporting ACOG's [American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists'] recommendation for vaccination of pregnant women to prevent more severe consequences from COVID." For RSV, Lundstrom recommended vaccination for adults aged 75 years and older, adults aged 50 to 74 years at high risk, and pregnant women. For newborns whose mothers were not vaccinated, monoclonal antibodies can provide protection against RSV, she said. Reference 1. Current Epidemic Trends (Based on Rt). CDC. September 18, 2026. Author(s)Sabrina McCrear, Tammy Lundstrom, MD, JD Fact checked by: Laura Joszt, MA Listen 0:00 / 0:00 Tammy Lundstrom, MD, JD, discusses the new childhood vaccine order, single-dose MMR access concerns, and the measles resurgence. Advertisement As the US records its highest number of measles cases in more than 3 decades, parents heading into fall are also navigating a federal overhaul of childhood vaccine guidance.1 An August executive order narrowed the list of diseases that all children should be vaccinated against from 18 to 11, moving influenza, COVID-19, hepatitis A and B, rotavirus, and meningococcal disease to shared clinical decision-making or risk-based recommendations. At the same time, measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccination coverage among kindergartners slipped to 92.4% in the 2025-2026 school year, while exemptions reached a record 4.2%.2 In an interview with The American Journal of Managed Care® (AJMC®), Tammy Lundstrom, MD, JD, senior vice president and chief medical officer at Trinity Health, discussed what these changes mean for families, why she sees single-dose MMR shots as an access problem, and how clinicians can build trust with hesitant parents. This interview has been lightly edited for clarity. AJMC: The August executive order narrows the list of diseases that all children are recommended to be vaccinated against to 11. It moves flu, COVID-19, hepatitis A and B, rotavirus, and meningococcal disease to shared clinical decision-making or risk-based recommendations. What does that mean for a parent trying to decide what their child needs this fall? Lundstrom: We're still following the previous recommendations and following the science. I think we've always, at least in my estimation, had shared decision-making for vaccines as providers, discussing with our patients the risks and benefits and the risks of not getting vaccinated, which are consequential, especially now with the measles outbreaks that we're seeing. Really, it's talking to parents about that. With hepatitis B for infants, I am old enough to have practiced in the era when we didn't have these vaccines, and I saw a lot of chronic liver disease in babies whose moms were hepatitis B carriers. Really, it's about having that conversation so that people truly understand from a scientific perspective what the risks and benefits are. AJMC: The order also calls for childhood vaccines to be given as single-disease shots rather than combination products when feasible, starting with splitting the MMR vaccine into 3 separate shots. From a clinical and access standpoint, what's your take on that? Lundstrom: I think from an access standpoint, it's problematic. We already know there's difficulty with getting access, and if you're talking about 3 visits instead of 1, that's taking parents away from work, trying to get 3 different appointments versus 1. I think the IDSA [Infectious Diseases Society of America] and American Academy of Pediatrics would agree that there's no benefit, from a scientific perspective, of getting 3 different injections versus 1. I think most pediatricians and most infectious disease doctors are still recommending getting the combined dose. The separate doses aren't even available in the US right now, so that complicates access and the recommendations. AJMC: The US is seeing its highest number of measles cases in more than 30 years, and nonmedical exemptions among kindergartners rose to 4.0% in the 2025-2026 school year. How worried are you about pockets of undervaccinated children, and what should a parent do if their child may have been exposed to measles? Lundstrom: I'm very worried about that, because I just saw data today from KFF showing that 92.4% of kindergartners are now vaccinated for MMR. And measles is one of the most contagious diseases that we have. We need at least 95% vaccination rates to provide herd immunity.2 That is very scary and problematic, especially in light of what I just heard today: Pennsylvania is nearing 800 cases, which is very, very concerning.4 I think if children are behind in vaccinations, now is a good time to get caught up. And if they've been exposed to measles, communicating with either public health or your primary care provider about the best options to try to prevent disease is the way to go. AJMC: You've led Trinity Health's pandemic response and spoken at town halls to counter misinformation. What approach works best when a hesitant parent comes to you with questions, and how do you keep trust when federal guidance and groups like the American Academy of Pediatrics are giving different advice? Lundstrom: It's really about the conversation, trying to understand people's fears. What are they afraid of? Do they understand the consequences if their child or somebody in their family gets one of these vaccine-preventable diseases? Many people are young enough that they haven't experienced the terrible consequences that can happen with some of these vaccine-preventable illnesses. Having factual conversations and trying to lay out the facts and the science is the best way to go forward. And then, like I said, try to understand the individual fear and address that. And myth-bust, too. We've done town halls, and we have myth-busting. A lot of what’s on social media isn’t scientifically accurate, so we’re trying to make sure people have the right information to make their decision. References Measles cases and outbreaks. CDC. Policy Points: Institutional trust appears to constitute an essential component of pandemic preparedness. Czech excess mortality—49% higher than Austria’s and approximately twice the European mean—illustrates that governance failures can undermine functional preparedness assets. The observed 8–10-week lag between trust decline and mortality divergence is consistent with a potential early-warning window. Regular monitoring of public trust may identify governance deterioration before preventable mortality escalates, thereby operationalizing trust as a measurable governance outcome. Competent health leadership continuity is a protective factor, not a guarantee. Five Czech health ministers in 15 months coincided with the deterioration in public cooperation, demonstrating how political instability weakens pandemic-response capacities even where technical preparedness exists. Context: The Czech Republic’s COVID-19 excess mortality represents a preparedness paradox. Despite entering the pandemic with substantial technical capacity—including the highest intensive care unit density in the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, an early national mask mandate, and an initially effective contact-tracing system—that country experienced age-standardized excess mortality of 15.24 per 10,000, approximately twice the European mean and 49% higher than neighboring Austria. Methods: This mixed-methods comparative case analysis examined relevant data from March 2020 through December 2023. Austria was chosen as a comparative governance benchmark to the Czech Republic because it closely matched that country’s initial governmental trust level (entering the pandemic within approximately two percentage points), and Slovakia is a historically and geographically proximate comparator. Age-standardized excess mortality was examined alongside government trust measures, mobility indicators, vaccination data, and policy stringency indices. Exploratory lag correlations assessed the temporal relationship between changes in trust and subsequent mortality. Findings: Czech governmental trust declined from approximately 71% to 19% during the pandemic period, among the largest declines in Europe. Austrian trust remained comparatively stable, whereas Slovakia also experienced a substantial decline in trust alongside high excess mortality. Czech mortality divergence from Austria emerged approximately 8–10 weeks after trust deterioration. Four mechanisms are proposed through which trust erosion may have influenced mortality: reduced compliance with public health measures, vaccine hesitancy, collapse of contact tracing, and governance-associated misperceptions of the scientific consensus. Conclusions: This analysis suggests that governance stability and institutional trust appear to function as important public health pandemic preparedness measures. content: News Sports Autos Entertainment Real Estate Advertise Obituaries eNewspaper Legals HEALTH Michigan, much of the U.S. in COVID-19 surge Kristen Jordan Shamus Detroit Free Press Sept. 23, 2026, 5:01 p.m. ET Hear this story The Pandemic Mitigation Collaboration analyzes wastewater data to show where COVID-19 is spreading most. This week, its updated map shows Michigan is now in a surge. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has changed the way it reports data on COVID-19, lowering the thresholds for what is considered low, moderate, high and very high levels. Experts suggest the time is now to get a COVID-19 vaccine, if you haven't already. As Michiganders weigh their seasonal vaccine options, COVID-19 cases are surging close to home and across much of the U.S. The Mitten is among at least 37 states and three territories are experiencing coronavirus outbreaks, according to the Pandemic Mitigation Collaborative's latest map, which was built using county-by-county data from wastewater samples. It notes: There likely are outbreaks in other states, too, where monitoring is poor, such as Maryland, Idaho, Louisiana and Tennessee. Here in Michigan, testing of wastewater samples from six Michigan communities show more people in the state had COVID-19 infections in the last week than at any time since March, according to WastewaterSCAN. Coronavirus activity was considered "high" as of Sept. 16 at collection sites in Ann Arbor, the city of Warren and Mount Pleasant. It was considered "moderate" in Jackson, Jenison and Traverse City, though the data suggests an upward trend. This means now is the time to get a COVID-19 vaccine, if you haven't already been boosted this season, said Michael Hoerger, who leads the collaborative at Tulane University, where he also is an associate professor of psychology, psychiatry and oncology. What type of COVID-19 vaccine should I get? The U.S. Food and Drug Administration authorized the following COVID-19 vaccines, which have been updated for the 2026-27 respiratory virus: Nuvaxovid: A protein-based vaccine made by Novavax and Sanofi, which can be used in people ages 65 and older as well as those between the ages of 12 and 64 with an underlying condition, such as asthma, cancer, diabetes or obesity, that puts them at higher risk for severe outcomes from COVID-19. Spikevax, an mRNA vaccine made by Moderna, which can be given to people ages 65 or older and to those who are between 6 months and 64 years old with at least one underlying condition that puts them at high risk for severe outcomes from COVID-19. Comirnaty, an mRNA COVID-19 vaccine made by Pfizer and BioNTech. It can be used in people ages 65 and older as well as anyone ranging from 5 years to 64 years old with at least one underlying condition that puts them at high risk for severe outcomes from COVID-19. mNexSpike, a lower-dose mRNA COVID-19 vaccine made by Moderna that can be used in people ages 65 and older as well as those between the ages of 12 and 64 who have an underlying condition that puts them at risk for severe disease with COVID-19 infection. CDC shifts how it reports COVID-19 spread Tracking COVID-19 spread six years after the pandemic began isn't as easy as it used to be, as reporting requirements have changed along with the way the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention maps the virus on its website. The federal agency has shifted its analysis of wastewater data in a way that minimizes the risk of infection, said Hoerger. "The CDC is blue washing to make COVID levels look artificially low," Hoerger said in a video posted on the collaborative's website. "They changed their color-coding scheme to make COVID levels look lower across the U.S. and there are further data anomalies that raise red flags. All of this leaves you less prepared. "The CDC monitors COVID transmission through wastewater and they take these numeric values and convert them to a color scheme in categories. About a year ago, they made a major update to the system that mostly pushed higher levels into lower categories. This [August], they did the exact same thing, but to a much greater degree." So, he explained, a level of COVID detection in wastewater that would have been considered very high in the past is now classified as just "high" on the CDC's surveillance map. Similarly, "moderate" spread is now considered "low," which is represented on the CDC's map as the color blue. "The CDC website is just less reliable for the casual user," Hoerger said. "We warned you that if any funny business like this ever happened, we would catch it right away. Here, we did." Hoerger and his team developed a heat map that shows county-by-county COVID-19 transmission using raw data collected from wastewater samples that can reveal a clearer picture of how much of the virus is spreading in communities, he said. It allows people to see the data the way it used to be classified, and to toggle to the system the CDC now is using to compare the differences. Changing federal vaccine recommendations, too It isn't only the data about COVID-19 spread that's changed at a federal level. President Donald Trump and Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the U.S. secretary of health and human services, have made dramatic changes to how the U.S. government reviews and recommends vaccines and issues guidelines for their use. Those efforts have sparked outrage among many in the scientific community, which led the major medical societies and associations to band together in collaboration with the Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy at the University of Minnesota to launch the Vaccine Integrity Project, which provides evidence-based data on the safety and efficacy of vaccines. “Vaccines are one of medicine’s greatest success stories,'' said Sarah C. Nosal, president of the American Academy of Family Physicians (AAFP) during an August news conference. "They prevent serious illness, reduce hospitalizations and long-term complications and save lives." Although they differ from the federal government's guidelines on COVID-19 vaccines, the AAFP's recommendations are closely aligned with those set by other medical societies, including the American Academy of Pediatrics and the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists, the Infectious Diseases Society of America and the American Medical Association, "to ensure continuity for both patients and physicians," Nosal said. Dr. Ronald Nahass, president of the Infectious Diseases Society of America, said at the news conference that all of the organizations are "speaking with one voice relative to the vaccinations and all acknowledging the challenges of the lack of trust and the lack of clarity. "The medical community ... is uniform in our effort to bring clarity and to restore that trust." They suggest: All adults 19 years of age and older should get an annual COVID-19 vaccine. It is especially important to get a COVID-19 vaccine if you are: 65 years and older; At an increased risk for severe COVID-19 infection; and Have never received a COVID-19 vaccine. All adults ages 65 years and older should get two doses of the updated COVID-19 vaccine. The first should be administered this fall. The second shot should follow six months later to maintain protection against the virus because immunity wanes over time. Infants and toddlers between the ages 6 months and 23 months should be vaccinated against COVID-19. Kids ages 2 years to 18 years old who are at risk for severe illness from COVID-19 infection should be vaccinated. The same is true for any children whose families choose to vaccinate against COVID-19. Anyone who is pregnant should get a COVID-19 vaccine during any trimester. Vaccination also is safe for women who are breast-feeding. Contact Kristen Shamus: kshamus@freepress.com. Subscribe to the Detroit Free Press. Symptoms Alone Can't Tell: Tammy Lundstrom, MD, JD Author(s)Sabrina McCrear, Tammy Lundstrom, MD, JD Fact checked by: Rose McNulty Overlapping COVID-19 and flu symptoms make diagnosis hard, says Trinity Health's Tammy Lundstrom, who outlines prevention and vaccine guidance. Advertisement Captions are auto-generated. COVID-19 infections are growing or likely growing in 27 states as of September 16, 2026, according to estimates from the CDC.1 As flu season begins, Tammy Lundstrom, MD, JD, senior vice president and chief medical officer at Trinity Health, said in an interview with The American Journal of Managed Care® that COVID-19 and flu symptoms overlap enough to make the 2 illnesses difficult to tell apart. Fatigue, muscle aches, fever, sore throat, cough, and shortness of breath are all symptoms associated with both COVID-19 and the flu, Lundstrom said. Children in particular may also experience gastrointestinal upset, including nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea, with COVID-19, she added. "Really, it's hard to distinguish just by symptoms what you're dealing with. It really requires a visit," Lundstrom said. To limit spread, she recommended staying home when sick, washing hands frequently, using antimicrobial hand gels, avoiding touching the nose, mouth, and eyes, and covering the mouth and nose when sneezing or coughing. Lundstrom also emphasized vaccination. She recommended the flu vaccine for anyone aged 6 months and older, with a high-dose or recombinant flu vaccine for adults older than 65 years. For COVID-19, she pointed to recommendations from the Infectious Diseases Society of America, the American Medical Association, and the American Academy of Pediatrics. "Anybody over the age of 19 should get vaccinated. Those 6 months of age to 23 months should be vaccinated for COVID," she explained. "And then older children are really based on their risk profile. And definitely, supporting ACOG's [American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists'] recommendation for vaccination of pregnant women to prevent more severe consequences from COVID." For RSV, Lundstrom recommended vaccination for adults aged 75 years and older, adults aged 50 to 74 years at high risk, and pregnant women. For newborns whose mothers were not vaccinated, monoclonal antibodies can provide protection against RSV, she said. Reference 1. Current Epidemic Trends (Based on Rt). CDC. September 18, 2026. content: Staff Login Email Send Feedback News Editorial Opinion Sports Features Saint Lucia Jazz Independence Election 2025 Arts & Entertainment Business Purpose and Profit Inspirational Inspiring Women Eulogy Saint Lucia Carnival Jobs / Notices Send Feedback Letters & Opinion COVID-19 Pandemic Reckoning: What the World Still Deserves to Know, and What Still Haunts the Living VP Digital4 days agoSeptember 23, 20260 Share Facebook Twitter LinkedIn WhatsApp Facebook Messenger Email By Dr. Clarence E. Pilgrim Six years after COVID-19 brought much of humanity to a standstill, the world has largely resumed its rhythm. Borders are busy, stadiums are full, aircraft crowd the skies, and masks have mostly disappeared. But normality is not resolution. The unfinished business of the pandemic is not only scientific; it is also moral, institutional, and deeply human. More than 779 million confirmed COVID-19 cases and over seven million deaths have been reported to the World Health Organization, which acknowledges that the true numbers are higher. Against a global population of approximately 8.3 billion people, few societies escaped the pandemic’s reach. Millions survived but did not fully recover. WHO estimates that about 6% of people with symptomatic COVID-19 develop Long COVID, with some experiencing respiratory, neurological, cardiovascular, and other problems for months or years. For them, the pandemic is not history. It still haunts the living. I understand something of its psychological reach personally. The pandemic made my circle of friends smaller and taught me to become apprehensive of even a friendly handshake—an instinct that remains with me today. After workplace exposure, I was immediately quarantined until testing confirmed that I was free of infection. The uncertainty, fear of becoming ill, concern about possibly exposing others, and suspicion of ordinary human contact reflected what millions experienced worldwide. COVID-19 changed more than health systems; for a time, it changed the meaning of proximity itself. A handshake, an embrace, or a conversation at close quarters became a potential source of danger. SARS-CoV-2 continues to circulate and evolve. WHO is monitoring variants including XFG, NB.1.8.1, PQ.16.1.1, and BA.3.2. The emergency ended; the virus did not. Neither did the questions surrounding its origin. The guilty plea of Dr. David Morens, a former senior adviser at the US National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, has reopened difficult questions about institutional credibility. Morens admitted involvement in efforts to evade federal public-record requirements relating to coronavirus research and official communications, including matters connected with a bat-coronavirus research grant involving the Wuhan Institute of Virology. These facts do not prove that SARS-CoV-2 escaped from a laboratory, nor do they establish criminal wrongdoing by Dr. Anthony Fauci. They do, however, establish that relevant official communications were deliberately concealed from normal transparency mechanisms. That warrants a simple question: Why? WHO’s scientific assessment says the weight of available evidence favours zoonotic spill-over. Yet important information remains unavailable, including early viral sequences, details concerning animals sold in Wuhan markets, and information about laboratory work and biosafety conditions. The responsible position is therefore neither to proclaim a laboratory origin proven nor dismiss it as impossible. Science should follow evidence, not defend predetermined conclusions. The same standard of evidence and transparency that should govern the origin debate must also govern how we assess the benefits and harms of vaccination. I chose to receive the COVID-19 vaccine and a booster because I trusted the recommendations of WHO and the international public-health community. There is strong evidence that vaccination reduced severe illness, hospitalization, and death. But acknowledging those benefits does not require denying genuine risks. Regulators across Europe, Africa, India, and Russia broadly reached the same conclusion: vaccines provided important protection, but continuing safety monitoring was necessary. European regulators recognized rare myocarditis and pericarditis after some mRNA vaccines. African authorities monitored rare clotting disorders. India recognized thrombosis with thrombocytopenia associated with adenovirus-vector vaccines while continuing surveillance of other reported conditions. Russia issued formal contraindications and clinical guidance. Across very different regulatory systems, the common lesson was not that vaccination was risk-free, but that benefit and risk had to be assessed together and continually. COVID-19 vaccines provided important protection, but risk was not zero. It should therefore be possible to say that vaccines saved lives without pretending that no one was harmed by them. It should also be possible to recognize genuine vaccine injuries without claiming that every illness or unexplained death following vaccination was caused by it. Those positions are not contradictory. They are the minimum requirements of intellectual honesty. In the United States, 11,055 claims alleging COVID-19 vaccine injury or death had been filed through the federal compensation programme by July 2026. A claim is not proof of causation, and many did not meet evidentiary requirements. Nevertheless, some vaccine-related injuries have been officially recognized. Where injury is scientifically established, those affected should not disappear behind statistics. Treat what can be treated. Rehabilitate where possible. Compensate fairly where responsibility is established. Human dignity should never be measured by prevalence. The same intellectual discipline applies to cardiovascular disease. WHO identifies cardiovascular disease as the world’s leading cause of death, a reality that long predates COVID-19. It cannot credibly be presented as proof of widespread vaccine injury. Yet legitimate questions remain. COVID-19 itself can affect the cardiovascular system. Long COVID may contribute to illness. Traditional risk factors and disrupted healthcare remain important. Rare vaccine-associated cardiovascular complications have also been documented. The question therefore is not whether vaccines caused post-pandemic cardiovascular disease, but how much illness resulted from COVID infection, existing disease, interrupted healthcare, or recognized vaccine complications. There is no credible global figure that answers that fully. The absence of an answer should encourage research, not speculation. History also warns us that another pandemic will come. Major respiratory pandemics struck in 1889–90, 1918, 1957, 1968, 2009, and 2019. Their timing was irregular, so no responsible formula can predict the next one. But another pandemic within the lifetime of much of today’s population is entirely plausible. The true reckoning, therefore, is not about vindicating one government, scientist, institution, or vaccine. It is about whether humanity learns enough to protect everyone better next time—the majority who benefit from effective medical interventions, the minority who may suffer genuine harm, the vulnerable, and generations yet unborn. Progress that protects millions while abandoning the few who are genuinely harmed is incomplete. Equally, concern for the injured cannot justify denying interventions that saved lives on a vast scale. The higher obligation is to pursue both: protection and accountability, scientific advancement and human dignity, institutional strength and transparency. I trusted the international public-health system enough to receive a vaccine and booster. That trust should never require silence. Science earns authority through evidence. Institutions earn legitimacy through transparency. Leadership earns confidence through accountability. The dead cannot demand answers. The living can. And before another pandemic tests humanity, we should establish what was right, acknowledge what was wrong, repair what can still be repaired, and build systems capable of protecting both the many and the few. The next response must be not merely faster, but wiser, fairer, more transparent, and directed toward the greatest good of all. content: Advanced Search Home News Releases Multimedia Meetings Login Register News Release 23-Sep-2026 UTHealth Houston database fills gap in Long COVID surveillance Peer-Reviewed Publication University of Texas Health Science Center at Houston Facebook X LinkedIn WeChat Bluesky Message WhatsApp Email image: During the pandemic, surveillance systems tracked COVID-19 cases, emergency department visits, hospitalizations and deaths. No similarly comprehensive surveillance system exists for Long COVID. (Photo by UTHealth Houston) view more Credit: UTHealth Houston UTHealth Houston researchers have found that Long COVID diagnoses varied significantly across populations and variant periods over a two-year period, revealing patterns that could help public health agencies and health systems better target follow-up and care, monitor long-term impacts, and allocate healthcare resources where they’re needed most. The analysis was published in the International Journal of Infectious Diseases. Researchers used the Texas All-Payer Claims Database, maintained by UTHealth Houston and the UTHealth Houston School of Public Health Center for Health Care Data, which covers nearly 60% of insured Texans, to examine patterns in Long COVID diagnoses across different populations and major SARS-CoV-2 variant periods from October 2021 to October 2023. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Long COVID is a chronic condition that occurs after SARS-CoV-2 infection and lasts at least three months. Although long COVID is more common among patients who experienced severe COVID-19 illness, it can affect anyone who has been infected. Because each SARS-CoV-2 infection carries a risk of Long COVID, repeated infections may continue to contribute to its overall burden. While fewer new cases are being reported than earlier in the pandemic, Long COVID remains a significant public health concern, affecting millions of U.S. adults and children. “We still do not have a clear picture of how often it is being diagnosed, which groups are most affected, or where the burden is highest,” said Boya Peng, a doctoral candidate in biostatistics at UTHealth Houston School of Public Health. During the pandemic, surveillance systems tracked COVID-19 cases, emergency department visits, hospitalizations and deaths. No similarly comprehensive surveillance system exists for Long COVID. Population-level estimates have often relied on self-reported surveys, which can be affected by who chooses to participate, how well people recall their symptoms, and differences in how Long COVID is defined. The Texas All-Payer Claims Database was established in 2021 by the 87th Texas Legislature. The database includes medical, pharmacy, and dental claims, along with eligibility and provider files, from private and public payers. It contains administrative claims information for approximately 60% of insured Texans and represents nearly all medical claims from health plans regulated by the state. Using this large, population-level resource, researchers were able to examine how documented Long COVID differed by age, sex, insurance type and geographic region across multiple COVID-19 variant periods. They found that Long COVID diagnoses generally followed waves of acute COVID-19 infection. Peaks in COVID-19-related emergency department visits typically preceded increases in Long COVID claims by two to three weeks. Older adults had substantially higher documented rates of Long COVID, especially those aged 70 years and older.. Medicare fee-for-service beneficiaries also had particularly high rates, and women had higher rates than men. Researchers also identified notable geographic differences in documented Long COVID rates and variation in the time between an initial COVID-19 encounter and a subsequent Long COVID diagnosis. Higher rates were observed in parts of the High Plains and Northwest Texas regions, and rural counties generally had higher documented Long COVID incidence than urban counties. Among patients who had previously visited an emergency department for COVID-19, the median time from that encounter to a Long COVID diagnosis was 22 days, compared with 26 days among patients whose COVID-19 care did not involve an emergency department visit. “Our main conclusion is that large health care claims databases such as the TX-APCD can help researchers understand the documented burden of Long COVID at the population level,” Peng said. “Claims data can complement surveys, electronic health records and traditional public health surveillance systems to support future planning for Long COVID care.” UTHealth Houston authors include Kaiming Bi, PhD; Dei'sharrah Allen-Benson; Yashar Talebi, MD; Samiran Ghosh, MD; Ashraf Yaseen, PhD; Melissa Valerio-Shewmaker, PhD; Eric Boerwinkle, PhD; Stacia M. DeSantis, PhD; Michael Swartz, PhD; Cecilia Ganduglia Cazaban, MD, PhD of UTHealth Houston School of Public Health. Kerem Yücel | MPR News 2023 Go Deeper. Create an account or log in to save stories. Log in Like this? Thanks for liking this story! We have added it to a list of your favorite stories. Show me! Save Share As respiratory virus season approaches, Minnesota clinics and pharmacies are offering updated COVID-19 and annual flu vaccines. But changing federal guidance has left some people uncertain about who should get vaccinated when. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved four updated COVID-19 vaccines in late August to target the latest circulating variants. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, however, has not issued new federal recommendations specifying who should get the shot. Instead, the agency is advising people to discuss COVID-19 vaccination with their healthcare provider. Conversely, major medical groups, as well as health officials from Children’s Minnesota and the Minnesota Department of Health, continue to recommend vaccination for most people. Health officials say vaccines are considered safe and remain the most effective tool for reducing the risk of severe illness and protecting those who are more vulnerable to respiratory viruses. Turn Up Your Support MPR News helps you turn down the noise and build shared understanding. Turn up your support for this public resource and keep trusted journalism accessible to all. Here’s what Minnesotans should know about COVID-19 and flu vaccines this fall: Who should get the COVID-19 vaccine? The American Academy of Family Physicians recommends that all adults age 19 and older receive an updated COVID-19 vaccine for the 2026-27 season. Vaccination is especially encouraged for pregnant people, young children, adults 65 and older and people at higher risk of severe illness. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends COVID-19 vaccination for all children ages 6 through 23 months. Although many children who contract COVID-19 experience mild illness, health officials caution that the virus can sometimes cause serious complications, including heart inflammation, respiratory complications and long COVID. Who should get the flu vaccine? The Minnesota Department of Health recommends an annual flu vaccine for everyone age 6 months and older. Adults 65 and older are encouraged to ask their health care provider about enhanced flu vaccine options, which are designed to produce a stronger immune response in people whose immune systems may not respond as strongly to standard vaccines. When should people get vaccinated? COVID-19 activity, including hospitalizations, remains relatively low nationally but has begun to increase, a pattern commonly seen in late summer and early fall. Health officials expect COVID-19, influenza and RSV to circulate this fall and winter, with respiratory virus activity generally increasing after the holidays. “Now is actually a really great time to get vaccinated before it's circulating and before we see that increase,” said Kate Kelly, Vaccines for Children program coordinator at the Minnesota Department of Health. Kelly said updated COVID-19 vaccines are arriving at Minnesota clinics and pharmacies. She advises residents to call ahead to confirm availability and consult with their healthcare provider or their child’s pediatrician about which vaccines are appropriate. Influenza follows a more predictable seasonal pattern compared to COVID-19, which can circulate throughout the year. Kelly recommends that adults get a flu shot in October to extend protection through the peak of flu season, but she said it is never too late to get vaccinated. Minnesota health officials typically see flu cases peak in January and February, so Kelly suggests that people who have not been vaccinated in October should still consider getting a flu shot in November or December. The American Academy of Pediatrics and the American Academy of Family Physicians recommend that children ages 8 and younger who may need two doses of the flu vaccine get vaccinated as soon as the vaccine becomes available. It takes around two to four weeks for the body to build an immune response after vaccination, according to Dr. Gigi Chawla of Children’s Minnesota. Chawla said vaccination helps protect individuals from illness while also protecting people in the community who are too young to be vaccinated or have health conditions that prevent them from receiving vaccines. She added that vaccination helps reduce the spread of respiratory viruses and said people who are sick should also stay home to avoid spreading the illness to others in the community. Where can Minnesotans get a COVID-19 or flu vaccine? Vaccines are readily available at Minnesota pharmacies, healthcare clinics and local health departments. Pharmacies typically cannot vaccinate children under 3, so health officials say parents of young children should consult their primary care provider about vaccinations. Most insurance plans cover the full cost of recommended vaccines. For adults age 19 and older who do not have insurance or whose insurance does not cover vaccines, there are clinics that serve uninsured and underinsured adults. Dr. Margot Savoy, chief medical officer of the American Academy of Family Physicians, says hospitals haven’t yet seen the kind of strain that hit last season. “We’re at the part of the season where we’re getting prepared... but luckily we’re not quite seeing those hospitalizations happen yet, which makes it a great time to get vaccinated before that season kicks off,” Savoy said. This year’s guidance is largely unchanged, with a few key updates: Flu: Still recommended for everyone 6 months and older. New this year is an mRNA-based flu vaccine option. RSV: Recommendations are the same for most groups, but pregnant patients now have a wider window — extended through March instead of January — after infections were still occurring that late last season. COVID-19: The vaccine has been updated to match circulating strains, but recommendations haven’t changed. Adults 18 and older should still get vaccinated, and those 65 and older may consider a second dose six months after the first, since COVID-19 circulates year-round. Because symptoms of flu, COVID-19 and RSV often overlap, Savoy recommends testing to know for sure. “The reality is that most of the time the best way to find out is to do a test,” she said. Home tests are widely available, and telehealth visits can help patients get treatment without leaving home. Those unsure of results can visit a doctor’s office — masked, to avoid spreading illness. All three vaccines, along with others like shingles, can be given in the same visit. “I just turned 50. I actually got as my birthday present COVID and RSV as well as influenza,” Savoy said. “It’s just a great time to get it done all at one time instead of having to think about it or remember it for later.” Beyond vaccination, Savoy recommends simple prevention habits: wash hands often, disinfect high-touch surfaces like doorknobs and sink handles, dispose of used tissues promptly, and wear a mask when sick or visiting a doctor’s office. content: 疫苗平台的发展:聚焦COVID-19大流行 《Acta Paediatrica》:Exploring the Development of Vaccine Platforms, With a Particular Focus on the COVID-19 Pandemic 【字体: 大 中 小 】 时间:2026年09月26日 来源:Acta Paediatrica 1.8 疫苗作为人类健康的基石已有200多年历史,并且是减少病原体导致的儿童死亡的最重要工具之一。疫苗的概念基本上是取某种安全的东西,使其具有免疫原性,并诱导宿主产生免疫反应,从而保护其免受危险病原体的侵害。两个世纪前,减毒活疫苗是唯一的选择。这些疫苗非常优秀,甚至可能是最佳的疫苗平台,但它们存在局限性,因为并非总能安全地给予所有人,例如由于免疫功能缺陷或怀孕。这就是为什么开发了更新的平台,如灭活疫苗。这些疫苗提供了更好的全面安全性,但通常免疫原性较低,需要额外剂量。20世纪80年代,亚单位疫苗问世。这些疫苗仅使用病毒的部分成分,进一步提高了安全性,并引入了利用基因技术生产疫苗的可能性。将基因疫苗加入工具箱彻底改变了研究人员应对COVID-19大流行的方法。宿主成为疫苗的生产者,更好地模拟了减毒活疫苗诱导的免疫反应。本小型综述将讨论所有这些平台。 1 Introduction 疫苗在200多年间减少了病原体导致的儿童死亡,但COVID-19大流行彻底改变了疫苗学。此前,针对新病毒的疫苗通常需要5~10年才能上市,且基于减毒活病毒、灭活全病毒和亚病毒成分等传统平台。基因疫苗在疫情前已发展10~20年,并进入II期临床试验。最早在美国和欧洲获批的三种COVID-19疫苗均为基因疫苗,分别基于信使核糖核酸(mRNA)或腺病毒载体,编码严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2型(SARS-CoV-2)的刺突蛋白,在病毒基因序列公布后12个月内获得条件批准。这一成就依赖于学术界、工业界、医疗部门和监管机构的广泛合作。 2 Classic Vaccine Platforms 2.1 Live Attenuated Viral Vaccines 减毒活疫苗是最古老的平台。最早的疫苗可追溯至人痘接种,后经詹纳使用牛痘病毒预防天花。减毒活疫苗通过在组织培养中连续传代使病毒减毒,感染细胞并激活免疫系统。它们能诱导强烈的B细胞、CD4+ T细胞和CD8+ T细胞反应以及免疫记忆,单次接种常可获得终身免疫。然而,该平台存在风险,如免疫缺陷者或孕妇无法安全使用,且病毒可能恢复毒力或与野生型重组。现有例子包括麻疹-腮腺炎-风疹(MMR)疫苗、口服脊髓灰质炎疫苗、黄热病疫苗和最近的一种基孔肯雅疫苗等。 2.2 Killed Whole Virus Vaccines 灭活全病毒疫苗于19世纪末为霍乱和鼠疫开发,通过加热、辐射、甲醛或β-丙内酯灭活病毒。索尔克在20世纪50年代开发了注射用脊髓灰质炎疫苗,但Cutter实验室事故导致监管加强。1965年,福尔马林灭活的呼吸道合胞病毒(RSV)疫苗在儿童中引起疫苗相关增强性呼吸道疾病,促使不良事件报告系统建立。该平台安全性好,但免疫原性较弱,需多次接种并常添加佐剂。实例包括中国COVID-19疫苗、流感疫苗、甲肝疫苗等。 2.3 Subcomponent Vaccines 亚单位疫苗仅含病毒的一个或多个部分。可通过培养病毒后纯化蛋白,或通过基因工程在细菌、昆虫或动物细胞中表达。最常用的成分是参与受体结合的蛋白,能诱导中和抗体和T细胞。首个亚单位疫苗是乙型肝炎疫苗,最初从慢性HBV感染者血浆中纯化表面抗原颗粒,随后采用基因修饰酵母生产。乙肝疫苗在出生时接种可提供>90%的保护效果。其他例子包括裂解流感疫苗、Novavax COVID-19疫苗和人乳头瘤病毒疫苗,后者基于病毒样颗粒(VLPs)。 3 New Vaccine Platforms 3.1 Genetic Vaccines 基因疫苗在过去30年中通过动物研究和早期临床试验得到探索。其核心机制是注射DNA或mRNA到体内,使细胞表达抗原。COVID-19大流行中的突破性进展是脂质纳米颗粒包裹的mRNA疫苗和非复制型腺病毒载体疫苗。mRNA疫苗在细胞质中直接翻译为疫苗蛋白;腺病毒载体将DNA递送至细胞核,转录后翻译。此外,DNA疫苗主要在印度使用。mRNA和DNA疫苗可以无限次接种,因为不会诱导针对递送平台的抗体;而腺病毒和痘病毒载体在单次接种后诱导中和抗体,从而限制重复使用。 Severe COVID-19 is not simply a matter of infected airway cells. In the sickest patients, the virus can help set off a destructive inflammatory loop, in which immune cells that should be fighting infection instead become part of the problem. A new study from researchers at Gladstone Institutes and the University of California, San Francisco (UCSF), identifies one viral protein, ORF8, as a key driver of that process. The paper, “Secreted ORF8 reprograms macrophages to enhance SARS-CoV-2 infection of lung epithelial cells,” was published in Science Advances. The work builds on earlier efforts by Gladstone and UCSF scientists to map interactions between SARS-CoV-2 proteins and human proteins in search of viral vulnerabilities that could be targeted with drugs. ORF8 had emerged as an intriguing but puzzling candidate. In isolated lung cells, ORF8 appeared to limit viral replication, yet SARS-CoV-2 variants lacking ORF8 have tended to cause milder disease. To resolve that contradiction, Melanie Ott, MD, PhD, director of the Gladstone Infectious Disease Institute, and colleagues focused on macrophages, immune cells that help shape the body’s response to infection and inflammation. The team exposed macrophages to ORF8, studied how the cells responded to SARS-CoV-2 infection, and then tested how those immune-cell changes affected nearby alveolar type II lung epithelial cells. They also evaluated ORF8’s effects in mice infected with SARS-CoV-2. The researchers found that ORF8 increased macrophage expression of angiotensin converting enzyme 2, or ACE2, the receptor SARS-CoV-2 uses to enter cells, making the immune cells more permissive to infection. Once infected, ORF8-exposed macrophages were more likely to lose antiviral function, undergo inflammatory cell death, and release signals that promoted lung inflammation and made surrounding lung epithelial cells more vulnerable to viral replication. “We were surprised to see how effectively ORF8 turns our own immune defenses against us,” said first author Yusuke Matsui, MD, PhD, a staff research scientist in Ott’s lab. “ORF8 is hijacking macrophages to enhance infection of the surrounding tissue.” In co-culture experiments, the presence of macrophages changed ORF8’s effect on infection. As the authors wrote in the paper, macrophage co-culture “overrides ORF8’s previously reported inhibition of AT2 [human alveolar type II] infection, restoring infectious viral production.” In mice, SARS-CoV-2 carrying ORF8 caused greater lung inflammation, viral burden, and scarring than virus lacking the protein, supporting the idea that ORF8 helps create a feedforward circuit linking immune-cell infection to lung pathology. The work also highlights a potential therapeutic target. Researchers tested brodalumab, an antibody already FDA-approved for psoriasis that blocks IL-17RA, the receptor previously linked to ORF8. In mice, IL-17RA blockade countered “ORF8 activity, lowering viral burden and attenuating pulmonary inflammation and fibrosis,” the authors wrote. Ott said the findings could support more targeted treatments for severe COVID-19. “By showing that this single viral protein is the main bridge between viral growth and tissue damage, we’ve found a clear target for new treatments,” she added. content: 波兰孕妇COVID-19疫苗依从性及其影响因素:一项横断面研究 《Frontiers in Public Health》:COVID-19 vaccine compliance among pregnant women in Poland during the pandemic 【字体: 大 中 小 】 时间:2026年09月25日 来源:Frontiers in Public Health 4.1 编辑推荐: 摘要 研究背景:本研究旨在评估SARS-CoV-2大流行期间波兰孕妇对COVID-19疫苗接种的依从性,并识别与疫苗接受度相关的因素。鉴于孕妇发生严重COVID-19并发症(包括急性呼吸衰竭、多器官衰竭以及孕产妇和新生儿死亡)的风险较高,了解影响免疫接种指南依 摘要 研究背景:本研究旨在评估SARS-CoV-2大流行期间波兰孕妇对COVID-19疫苗接种的依从性,并识别与疫苗接受度相关的因素。鉴于孕妇发生严重COVID-19并发症(包括急性呼吸衰竭、多器官衰竭以及孕产妇和新生儿死亡)的风险较高,了解影响免疫接种指南依从性的因素对于优化母婴公共卫生策略至关重要。 研究方法:这项横断面研究分析了2021年11月至2022年2月期间在格但斯克大学临床中心新生儿科住院的675名女性所填写的问卷。分析评估了疫苗接种状态和疫苗类型与人口统计学特征、居住地以及产科病史(包括生育障碍和既往流产)之间的关联。 研究结果:数据显示,超过50%的受访者在妊娠期间接种了COVID-19疫苗。多变量分析显示,较低的教育程度是与较低疫苗接种几率最一致的相关因素。在特定模型中,较高年龄和大城市居住与较高的疫苗接种几率相关,而产科病史与疫苗接种状态无显著关联。 研究结论:虽然疫苗接受度处于中等水平,但研究结果突显了显著的人口学差异。这些发现表明,在产前保健期间,针对教育程度较低的女性开展个体化、循证的疫苗沟通尤为重要。 论文解读:波兰孕妇COVID-19疫苗依从性及其相关因素 **研究背景与意义** 2019冠状病毒病(COVID-19)大流行自2020年3月被世界卫生组织(WHO)宣布以来,对全球公共卫生构成严峻挑战。严重急性呼吸综合征冠状病毒2(SARS-CoV-2)具有高度传染性,可导致易感人群出现呼吸衰竭、多器官衰竭甚至死亡。孕妇作为特殊群体,感染SARS-CoV-2后发生严重并发症的风险显著升高,包括急性呼吸衰竭、多器官衰竭以及孕产妇和新生儿死亡率增加。为应对疫情,多种技术路线的疫苗被紧急授权使用,包括辉瑞/BioNTech和Moderna开发的核苷修饰信使核糖核酸(mRNA)疫苗,以及牛津/阿斯利康(Vaxzevria)和强生(Jcovden)的腺病毒载体疫苗。波兰妇产科医师协会(PTGiP)于2021年4月发布了孕妇接种COVID-19疫苗的推荐意见。然而,自20世纪90年代末以来,全球范围内对疫苗的怀疑态度日益增加,疫苗信心显著下降,尤其在波兰等中东欧国家。孕妇群体中的疫苗接种率本就偏低,而关于波兰孕妇对COVID-19疫苗的接受度、依从性以及感染发病情况,此前的医学报告中缺乏相关数据。因此,本研究旨在填补这一知识空白,评估孕妇对PTGiP推荐意见的依从性,并分析影响疫苗接种决策的社会人口学和产科因素,为优化母婴公共卫生策略提供循证依据。 **研究内容与结论概述** 研究人员在波兰格但斯克大学临床中心(UCC)新生儿科开展了一项横断面研究,调查了2021年11月18日至2022年2月28日期间住院的产后女性。研究共纳入675名符合条件并知情同意的妇女,通过结构化问卷收集其既往SARS-CoV-2感染史、COVID-19疫苗接种状态、人口学特征及产科病史(包括生育障碍和既往流产)。结果显示,超过一半的受访者(57.5%)在妊娠前或妊娠期间接种过COVID-19疫苗,其中最大的接种群体为仅在妊娠期间接种的妇女(35.3%)。多变量logistic回归分析表明,较低教育程度是与较低疫苗接种几率最一致且最稳健的独立预测因素;较高年龄(≥36岁)和大城市居住仅在特定模型中与较高接种几率显著相关,而产科病史(胎次、流产史)与疫苗接种状态无显著关联。研究结论强调,在产前保健中应对教育程度较低的孕妇开展针对性、循证的疫苗沟通,以提升疫苗接受度和覆盖率。该研究为波兰孕妇COVID-19疫苗决策的社会人口学差异提供了重要的基线数据,也为未来优化围产期免疫策略指明了方向。 **主要技术方法** 本研究为横断面问卷调查,样本来自波兰格但斯克大学临床中心新生儿科2021年11月18日至2022年2月28日住院的产后妇女(n=675),排除因波兰语语言障碍(14人)和资料不完整(2人)者。问卷为纸版匿名自愿填写,包含12个封闭式问题。统计分析采用Statistica 9.1软件,分类变量以频数和百分比表示,组间比较使用卡方(χ2)独立性检验,显著性水平设定为p<0.05。采用多变量logistic回归分析评估疫苗接种状态与人口学和临床变量的关联,计算校正后优势比(aOR)及95%置信区间(CI),并报告Nagelkerke R2。研究遵循《赫尔辛基宣言》和STROBE声明,经格但斯克医科大学伦理委员会批准(编号NKBBN/367/2021)。 **研究结果** **参与者特征与总体接种情况** 研究队列中,初产妇占51%,经产妇占49%;53%居住在大城市(>50万居民),21.6%居住在农村;年龄分布以26–35岁组为主(68.7%);大学以上教育程度者占69.3%。总体来看,388人(57.5%)在妊娠前或妊娠期间接种过COVID-19疫苗,287人(42.5%)从未接种。在接种疫苗的亚组中,仅在妊娠期间接种者占61.3%(n=238),仅在妊娠前接种者占14.7%(n=57),妊娠前和妊娠期间均接种者占24.0%(n=93)。在妊娠前已接种的150名女性中,38%未在妊娠期间完成全程接种。在妊娠前和妊娠期间均接种疫苗的93名女性中,妊娠期间接种的剂次发生在第三孕期者占57%,第二孕期占30.1%,第一孕期占19.4%(后者不符合PTGiP建议);另有6.5%的妇女在多个孕期记录了接种。在仅于妊娠期间接种疫苗的238名女性中,21.8%(n=52)在妊娠早期至少接受过一次接种,不符合PTGiP指南。绝大多数妊娠期间接种者使用辉瑞疫苗(91.8%),其次为阿斯利康(4.8%)、莫德纳(2.1%)和强生(1.8%)。所有在妊娠前接种辉瑞疫苗的妇女在妊娠期间均续用同一疫苗。在妊娠前和妊娠期间均接种的妇女中,20.4%从其他疫苗更换为辉瑞疫苗,符合PTGiP推荐。 **SARS-CoV-2感染率** 在整个队列中,25%(95% CI 21.9–28.4%)的受访者报告在妊娠前感染过COVID-19,12.4%(95% CI 10.2–15.2%)在妊娠期间感染。仅在妊娠期间接种疫苗的妇女中,妊娠前感染率为25.7%,妊娠期感染率为8.8%;仅在妊娠前接种疫苗的妇女中,相应感染率分别为28.7%和14.7%。 **教育程度与疫苗接种** 教育程度与疫苗接种意愿显著相关。在妊娠期间接种疫苗的受访者中,82.5%具有大学学历,16.3%为中学学历,1.2%为小学学历;而在未接种疫苗组中,56.7%为大学学历,38.4%为中学学历,4.9%为小学学历(χ2(2, N=675)=53.53,p<0.001,Cramér's Update on COVID-19 and flu vaccines; new study examines Latino economic mobility; remembering Paul Bender Sept. 22 More from this show On this episode of “Arizona Horizon,” Dr. Joel Terriquez, Medical Director for the Division of Public Health Preparedness at the Arizona Department of Health Services, discussed a statewide standing order for the 2026–27 flu season. The order allows pharmacists to give COVID-19 and flu vaccines to Arizonans without individual prescriptions. We also heard from Karen Armknecht, Vice President of Research and Evaluation for Chicanos Por La Causa, who discussed their new study on economic development for Latino communities. Research found inequality in Latino homeowners, credit card holders, higher education and more. Finally, Stephen Montoya, attorney at Montoya, Lucero and Pastor, discussed the legacy of Paul Bender, former professor of law and dean emeritus of the Sandra Day O’Connor College of Law at ASU. Bender taught extensively on both U.S. and Arizona constitutional law, serving as an expert on the U.S. Supreme Court for local, state and national media. In this segment: Dr. Joel Terriquez, Medical Director, Division of Public Health Preparedness, Arizona Department of Health Services Karen Armknecht, Vice President of Research and Evaluation, Chicanos Por La Causa Stephen Montoya, Attorney, Montoya, Lucero and Pastor Also in this episode: New Chicano Por La Causa study highlights financial disparities in Latino community Arizona Department of Health Services issues standing order for COVID-19 and flu vaccines Remembering the life and legacy of Paul Bender SPOTLIGHT Deadline extended! A systematic review and multi-level meta-analysis 【字体: 大 中 小 】 时间:2026年09月27日 来源:Journal of Public Health 3.5 编辑推荐: 摘要 目的:综合纵向、个体内证据,评估COVID-19疫情对社区居住老年人心理健康与心理幸福感的影响,并考察人口学、方法论及国家层面的调节变量。 方法:遵循注册方案及系统综述与Meta分析优先报告条目(PRISMA)指南,研究人员检索了世界卫生组织(WHO)C 摘要 目的:综合纵向、个体内证据,评估COVID-19疫情对社区居住老年人心理健康与心理幸福感的影响,并考察人口学、方法论及国家层面的调节变量。 方法:遵循注册方案及系统综述与Meta分析优先报告条目(PRISMA)指南,研究人员检索了世界卫生组织(WHO)COVID-19研究数据库(整合24个电子数据库),纳入评估2020年3月前后平均年龄≥60岁社区居住成年人的纵向研究。75项研究符合纳入标准。采用基于稳健方差估计的多水平随机效应Meta分析合并标准化均数差(SMD)。 结果:疫情与抑郁(SMD=0.23;95%CI [0.09–0.36];k=31)、焦虑(SMD=0.24;95%CI [0.03–0.45];k=22)和压力(SMD=0.22;95%CI [0.08–0.37];k=5)的小幅但显著增加相关,而孤独感的增幅更大(SMD=0.40;95%CI [0.10–0.69];k=20)。调节变量分析提示,75岁以上及欧洲以外地区的老年人恶化程度更大,但未达到统计显著性。 结论:疫情导致老年人心理健康出现小幅但可靠的下降,孤独感显著加剧,而心理韧性和社交活动保持稳定。这些估计值捕捉了晚年生活中强制性社会隔离的心理代价——此类状况在流行病、灾难及其他紧急情况下反复出现。随着人口老龄化及此类事件日益频繁,这些发现为危机应对中保护社会联系提供了持久的证据基础。 引言 COVID-19疫情将老年人置于全球危机的中心。60岁及以上成年人面临严重患病和死亡的显著升高风险,因此受到最严格和最持久的公共卫生措施限制,包括防护、物理距离以及社区和家庭活动的暂停。对于社会参与和日常生活规律对心理功能至关重要的群体而言,这些措施构成了一场深刻的自然实验:即对晚年社会生活条件的突然、全人群范围的改变。 理论提出了两种相互竞争的预测。第一种预测认为会造成伤害。在压力过程模型中,主要压力源会扩散到生活各领域的次级压力;疫情正是如此,产生了孤独感、照护中断和丧亲之痛,这些都是晚年抑郁和焦虑的既定风险因素。资源守恒理论也指向同一方向:该理论认为,当有价值的资源丧失且无法重建时,会产生心理困扰;而疫情为老年人创造了这些条件,剥夺了社会接触、体育活动和医疗保健,同时限制措施阻止了其恢复。第二种预测则认为存在心理韧性。社会情绪选择理论认为,随着时间视野缩短,老年人能更有效地调节情绪;而力量与脆弱性整合模型(SAVI)则界定了这种优势的边界:它依赖于个体能够构建自身环境并回避压力源的能力——而这恰恰是封锁措施所剥夺的。SAVI因此预测,在短暂或可控的压力下幸福感得以维持,但在持续、不可避免的压力下优势会被侵蚀。早期研究结果支持了这两种观点。 验证哪种观点正确需要大多数疫情研究无法提供的证据。大多数研究采用横断面设计,仅在2020年3月之后收集数据,这无法区分疫情相关变化与既有的症状水平;回顾性报告则易受回忆偏倚影响。理论辩论所需的推论——即老年人是否相对于自身的疫情前基线发生了变化——只能通过评估同一批个体在疫情爆发前后的纵向研究得出。现有的综合最多只提供了部分检验。早期的Meta分析汇总了横断面的患病率估计;纵向综合分析考察了一般成人样本,其中老年人仅构成一个小子组;或仅关注单一结局如孤独感。迄今为止最全面的年龄特异性综述将纵向研究与重复横断面研究混合在一起,从而混淆了个体内变化与人群水平的比较,纳入了临床和机构样本,并且搜索截止至2022年4月。值得注意的是,其纵向子集产生的效应大于横断面子集,这突显了进行严格个体内综合的必要性。此外,尚无既往综述考察过完整的主观幸福感结局范围,包括睡眠、认知、社会活动和行动能力,也未建模决定压力源强度和可控性的国家层面条件,如国民收入、疫苗接种覆盖率和预期寿命。这些问题非但没有减弱反而变得更加紧迫,因为新兴证据表明,老年人的心理健康在疫情爆发数年之后仍未恢复到疫情前水平。 本研究通过系统综述和多水平元分析(MLMA)填补上述空白,纳入评估2020年3月前后平均年龄≥60岁社区居住成年人的纵向研究。研究人员综合了两个维度的个体内变化:心理健康(抑郁、焦虑、压力、睡眠问题、认知和自我评价心理健康)和心理幸福感(孤独感、生活满意度、心理韧性、社会活动和行动能力)。结局选择基于前述理论考虑以及纵向队列研究中报告最一致的结局领域。次要目标是考察可能解释研究间异质性的人口学、方法论和国家层面调节变量,包括年龄、性别、世界区域、国民收入、疫苗接种覆盖率和预期寿命。通过限定纳入个体内证据并对嵌套效应量进行建模,本综述提供了疫情对老年人心理健康和幸福感影响的严谨估计,以及对晚年脆弱性与心理韧性竞争性理论的直接实证检验。 方法 本综述方案已在约克大学PROSPERO注册,注册号为CRD42024396898。研究遵循系统综述与Meta分析优先报告条目(PRISMA)指南进行。 纳入标准:报告(i)在COVID-19疫情爆发(2020年3月)前后收集数据的纵向设计;(ii)平均年龄≥60岁的社区居住老年人样本;(iii)与心理健康和心理幸福感相关的结局;(iv)标题和摘要可用英文获取。纳入已发表和未发表的来源。为保持一致性,排除了针对机构化人群的研究。 信息来源与检索策略:主要检索来源是世界卫生组织(WHO)COVID-19研究数据库,该数据库整合了来自24个电子数据库的记录。检索词结合了受控词汇和自由文本关键词,涉及老年人、COVID-19、心理健康和心理幸福感,并使用布尔运算符和通配符优化检索。补充来源包括Google Scholar、高相关性期刊的手工检索以及已发表系统综述的参考文献回溯。检索于2023年进行,纳入符合标准的稿件。所有记录使用基于网络的Covidence软件管理,检索程序遵循PRISMA指南。 数据收集过程:筛选分两个阶段进行。第一阶段,对标题和摘要进行相关性筛选。随机选取20%的记录由两名经过培训的评审员双盲筛选,差异通过讨论解决。其余80%由一名评审员筛选。第二阶段,所有全文由两名盲法评审员独立审查,分歧通过共识解决。 数据提取:数据提取至Covidence的结构化编码手册,包括研究设计、样本特征和结局测量。提取的统计量用于计算标准化均数差(SMD)。只有当至少三项研究报告了某一结局的结果时,才将其纳入Meta分析。缺失数据通过联系通讯作者处理,因信息缺失而被排除的研究不到2%。 效应量估计:原始研究中报告为连续数据的结局被转换为SMD,以便跨不同测量尺度进行综合。所有提取数据导出至RStudio。使用metafor包和clubSandwich估计器进行多水平元分析(MLMA),以说明研究间的固有依赖性和潜在嵌套数据结构。分析以叙述性描述及森林图和汇总表形式报告。异质性使用Tau平方、Q统计量和I平方进行评估,并进行调节变量分析。 质量偏倚风险:两名研究人员使用改编版纽卡斯尔-渥太华量表(NOS)对纳入队列研究的潜在偏倚风险进行了严格评估,该量表评估三个关键领域:研究组的选择、可比性和结局的确定。 调节变量分析:为解决异质性,调节变量分析包括人口学变量以及研究的方法学特征。 结果 对24个数据库的全面检索及补充检索共产生10,109条标题。剔除158条重复后,剩余9951项研究。在标题/摘要筛选中排除8979项,获得972篇全文待审。在此阶段,897篇被排除,最常见的原因是研究设计错误和结局错误。事实上,57%的研究因报告了非纵向的设计而被排除。其他研究因报告了本综述范围之外的结局而被排除。最终,75篇记录符合纳入标准。 评分者间信度:Cohen's Kappa为0.88,反映了两名编码者之间的高度一致性。 纳入文献特征:75篇综述研究的发表频率呈明显上升趋势,7%发表于2020年,43%发表于2021年,50%发表于2022年,1%发表于2023年。几乎均为同行评议期刊文章,主要以英文发表。地理分布上,欧洲贡献最大,其次是北美和亚洲,无研究源自非洲。多数研究在中高收入和高收入国家开展。定量纵向设计占主导地位,随机抽样是最常用的方法。 质量/偏倚风险:在本研究中,48项研究报告低偏倚风险,其余22项报告中等风险。主要局限体现在结局评估和失访项目上。在纳入的纵向研究中,结局并非基于盲法评估或医疗记录。相反,88%的研究中,参与者通过心理健康和幸福感的有效量表自我报告结局。在失访方面,少数研究失访率超过40%。在考虑了数据的嵌套结构后,研究人员发现较高的偏倚风险与较小的效应量相关。 多水平元分析:分别进行了Meta分析以评估疫情前后老年人心理健康和幸福感的变化。第一个维度聚焦心理健康。结果显示:抑郁症状出现小幅但统计学显著的增加;压力症状出现显著增加;焦虑症状出现统计学显著的增加;睡眠问题出现非常微小且不显著的增加;自我报告心理健康出现小幅、不显著的恶化;认知表现出现小幅、不显著的下降。 幸福感结局:研究人员进行了独立的多水平随机效应Meta分析,以评估疫情对心理韧性、孤独感、生活满意度、社会活动和行动能力的影响。结果显示:心理韧性无明显变化;孤独感出现显著增加;生活满意度出现不显著的下降;社会活动出现小幅不显著的下降;行动能力出现较大但不显著的下降。 发表偏倚:研究人员使用Egger回归的多水平扩展法检验了小研究效应。对于至少有十项研究的结局进行了检验。任何结局均未出现显著的小研究效应,表明不存在实质性的报告偏倚证据。 讨论 本系统综述和多水平元分析(MLMA)综合了75项关于COVID-19疫情对社区居住老年人心理健康和心理幸福感的个体内纵向证据。四项发现尤为突出。第一,疫情与抑郁症状、焦虑和压力的小幅但显著增加相关。第二,孤独感出现了最大的恶化,这是距离政策最直接针对的结局。第三,其余结局未显示显著变化,但这种不显著性在不同结局中含义不同。第四,调节变量分析揭示了少量显著效应,但出现了一致的模式:75岁以上成年人、非欧洲国家和低收入环境中恶化程度更大,同时更高的疫苗接种率与较低的抑郁水平之间存在边际关联。 这些结果既不支持统一的心理健康危机,也不支持简单的心理韧性,而是呈现了一种与理论预期密切吻合的分化模式。力量与脆弱性整合模型(SAVI)预测,在持续的、不可控制的压力源下,老年人的调节优势会被削弱,而对于那些可通过内部调节处理的结局则保持完好。孤独感在很大程度上取决于外部约束,任何调节策略都无法抵消,因此显示出最大的增长;心理健康结局适度恶化,这与真实但得到缓冲的压力反应一致;而心理韧性基本保持不变。心理健康变化的幅度与一般成人人群的Meta分析结果趋同,表明尽管老年人承担着最大的客观风险和最具限制性的措施,但其情况并未显著差于较年轻的人群。然而,本研究的估计值超过了Sch?fer等人报告的老年人困扰增加的综合效应。这一差异与其设计选择一致:他们的综合将纵向研究与重复横断面研究相结合,而其纵向子集产生的效应大于横断面子集,表明混合设计合并会削弱个体内变化。本研究结果反驳了早期评论的警报,同时确认了有意义的恶化确实发生了。 孤独感的增加尤其值得关注。它显著超过了先前对一般人群以及混合设计的老年人群体的合并估计。 相关新闻 生物通微信公众号 生物通新浪微博 微信 新浪微博 我要投稿 搜索 国际 国内 人物 产业 热点 科普 热搜:COVID-19|老年人|心理健康|孤独感|纵向研究|多水平元分析 热点排行 今日动态 | 人才市场 | 新技术专栏 | 中国科学人 | 云展台 | BioHot | 云讲堂直播 | 会展中心 content: COVID-19患者血栓栓塞事件分析及其相关因素:一项回顾性队列研究 《Journal of Vascular Nursing》:Thromboembolism analysis and associated factors in patients with COVID-19: retrospective cohort study 【字体: 大 中 小 】 时间:2026年09月27日 来源:Journal of Vascular Nursing 0.9 COVID-19患者除呼吸系统受累外,还可能出现全身性并发症。COVID-19相关血栓栓塞是一种具有可测量发病率并对住院照护产生重要影响的临床相关疾病。合并症、呼吸衰竭和心脏改变与血栓栓塞风险相关,凸显了其多因素性质。 严重急性呼吸综合征(Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome, SARS)是COVID-19的主要并发症之一。虽然该疾病最初以呼吸系统表现为特征,但整个疫情期间累积的证据表明,SARS-CoV-2感染还与止血和炎症改变密切相关,这些改变可促进血栓形成,累及动脉和静脉系统,尤其是在重症监护病房(Intensive Care Unit, ICU)收治的患者中。据估计,约20%至50%的住院COVID-19患者存在凝血异常;研究报道静脉血栓栓塞(Venous Thromboembolism, VTE)的患病率约为30%,其中深静脉血栓(Deep Vein Thrombosis, DVT)和肺栓塞(Pulmonary Embolism, PE)是最常见且具有临床意义的表现。尸检研究也证实,死于COVID-19的患者存在明显的高凝状态,肺栓塞发生率介于19%至33%之间,DVT可达58%。尽管关联明确,但关于最佳血栓预防方案、抗凝策略以及COVID-19相关凝血功能障碍的管理仍未达成共识。此外,在巴西社会脆弱和经济欠发达地区,相关流行病学数据仍然稀缺。考虑到血栓栓塞事件的高发性、预防和治疗策略的不足,以及其对医院服务的负担,本研究旨在评估COVID-19患者住院期间血栓栓塞的发生率及其相关危险因素。 研究人员采用回顾性队列研究设计,按照观察性流行病学研究报告规范(Strengthening the Reporting of Observational Studies in Epidemiology, STROBE)进行。研究于2020年3月至2021年12月在巴西米纳斯吉拉斯州迪亚曼蒂纳的Santa Casa de Caridade de Diamantina转诊医院开展。该医院位于历史上以社会脆弱性和经济不平等为特征的Jequitinhonha Valley地区,是多个城市的区域转诊中心。研究纳入815例确诊COVID-19并入住ICU或急诊单元(Emergency Unit, EU)的成人患者的医疗记录。数据由两名经过培训的研究人员从病历中提取,暴露变量包括性别、年龄、症状、合并症、吸烟饮酒史、手术史、血栓预防措施等;主要结局为住院期间发生血栓栓塞事件(包括VTE和动脉血栓事件)。统计分析采用Stata 16.0软件,使用描述性统计、Pearson卡方检验或Fisher精确检验、Mann-Whitney U检验、Kaplan-Meier生存曲线、log-rank检验以及Cox比例风险回归模型。研究经研究伦理委员会批准(意见编号4,896,042)。 主要结果如下: 总体发生率与基线特征:在815例患者中,49例(6.01%)发生血栓栓塞事件。有无既往血栓栓塞史两组在年龄、入住地点、饮酒、合并症、既往手术史、入院时心脏和呼吸状况及血栓预防措施等方面存在差异。 既往血栓栓塞史与再发风险:有既往血栓栓塞史的患者发生新血栓栓塞事件的比例更高。Kaplan-Meier曲线显示,两组无事件生存概率差异具有统计学意义(log-rank检验p=0.0406)。发生事件的患者中,无既往血栓栓塞史者的中位住院时间为11天(四分位距[Interquartile Range, IQ] 5-18),而有既往史者为10天(IQ 6-14)。
